strengths: Addresses an important issue for multilingual NLP: Wikipedia size and reputation can obscure substantial redundancy. The reported filtering statistics and correlation with independently estimated bot-article prevalence provide useful evidence.
The experimental scope is substantial, covering 50 languages in monolingual SIB200 evaluation, several African-language tasks, XLM-R adaptation, and multilingual pretraining on 100 Wikipedias.

The detailed results support a useful narrower finding: primary filtering often preserves monolingual performance despite substantial pruning, with improvements for some languages. The discussion of script-switching failures and task-dependent outcomes appropriately challenges universal filtering recommendations.
The linked filtering, tokenization, and training pipeline, together with hyperparameter tables and per-language results, provides valuable infrastructure for further research.
weaknesses: The random control is insufficiently specified to establish the benefit of quality selection. Section 5.1 samples as many articles as primary filtering removes, without clearly stating whether these sampled articles are retained or discarded. If retained, this mismatches corpus sizes. Report retained article/token counts and use controls matched to each pruning level. Changes in tokenizers and epoch-based training budgets also limit attribution specifically to text quality.

The multilingual Belebele evaluation is largely uninformative: Table 15 averages approximately 0.25 for every condition, including near-chance English performance on this four-choice task. Small differences around chance cannot substantiate preservation or improvement of useful reading comprehension. Table 13's adaptation improvement from 0.25 to 0.30 is more encouraging, but lacks uncertainty estimates. Verify the English fine-tuning baseline and repeat these evaluations before drawing broad zero-shot recommendations.

Important reporting inconsistencies undermine confidence. Averaging Table 11 gives approximately 0.632 raw, 0.630 primary, 0.621 heuristic, and 0.502 random; Table 2 instead assigns 0.63 to random and 0.50 to heuristic. Moreover, raw and heuristic uncertainty values are identical in all 50 Table 11 rows. The summaries and uncertainties need verification against run-level results.

The quality taxonomy is only partially validated. Clustering filtering rates establishes susceptibility to these filters, rather than general linguistic quality. Foreign-script material, templatic articles, and bot authorship are not intrinsically unusable. A systematic assessment of retained and removed samples by proficient speakers would help validate filter precision and tier interpretations. Likewise, the KDE thresholding procedure lacks calibration or sensitivity analysis showing that distributional extremes identify undesirable text.

The efficiency and performance-preservation claims exceed the evidence. Multilingual models receive the same 200,000 training steps, so reducing unique corpus size does not itself demonstrate reduced training compute. Fixed-epoch experiments plausibly save compute, but processed tokens, actual training costs, and filtering overhead are unreported. Furthermore, the nonsignificant pruning–accuracy correlation in Section 6 does not establish performance equivalence; XNLI averages decrease under both filtering settings.

Reproducibility remains incomplete in the manuscript despite the repository link: the Wikipedia snapshot and extraction configuration, MinHash shingling/permutation settings, KDE bandwidth, and exact combination of heuristic filters are unspecified. Appendix A also assigns the random condition the filtered tokenizer, conflicting with the explanation that it retains Latin tokenization for ary. These ambiguities, together with the control and evaluation problems, require important revisions before a sound Findings recommendation.
